opus-5.5.text:
I think you have to separate two questions: whether the valuation is justified by today's fundamentals, and whether the bet itself makes sense. On the first, clearly not. No humanoid company today has revenue, deployment scale, or product maturity anywhere near what a 30 or 40 billion dollar number implies. So if you look at it as a conventional company, it doesn't add up.

But investors at that level aren't buying the present. They're buying an option on what may be the largest market ever, which is general-purpose physical labor. If you believe that within ten or fifteen years a general robot can do a meaningful share of the work humans do in factories, warehouses, retail, and eventually homes, then the addressable market is measured in trillions. Against that, even a few tens of billions is a relatively small bet, especially if you think the market will consolidate around a handful of winners, the way large language models have concentrated around a few frontier labs.

The second part of the logic, I think, is the analogy to AI. People watched OpenAI go from a research lab to an enormous valuation, and many feel they missed that. Embodied intelligence is widely seen as the next frontier after language models. So there's a strong fear of missing out, and capital is willing to pay a premium for teams that look like they could be the "OpenAI of robotics." Figure has been very good at telling that story: the humanoid form factor, partnerships with automakers, rapid demos, and a founder who raises money aggressively and moves fast.

Now, as someone who works on this both in research and in a company, I'd add a few cautions. First, the hardest problem is not the body, it's the brain. Generalization in the physical world is far harder than in language, mainly because of data. We don't have an internet of robot actions. So the real question for any company is how it solves the data problem, whether through large-scale simulation, synthetic data, teleoperation, or real-world deployment that creates a data flywheel. A valuation story that depends on demos rather than a credible data strategy is fragile.

Second, commercialization has to come in stages. You can't jump straight to the home robot that does everything. The companies that survive will find scenarios today where robots are already reliable enough to create real value, such as picking and placing in retail or logistics, get units deployed, collect data, and iterate. That's how you turn a story into a business.

So my view is that the positive case is real at the level of the industry: if general-purpose robots work, the value created is enormous, and a few companies will be worth far more than 40 billion. But whether any specific company deserves that price depends on whether it can convert capital into a genuine technical lead, especially in data and generalization, and into real deployments, before the money and patience run out. Right now the market is pricing the dream. The next few years will show who can actually deliver it.

r001.rationale: The response says the addressable market for general-purpose robots could be measured in trillions if they perform human work in factories and other settings. It does not argue that a humanoid company’s valuation could reach the trillions; it only says a few companies could be worth far more than $40 billion.

fable-5.1.text:
I think you have to look at it from the perspective of what the market is pricing in. At 30 or 40 billion, you're not paying for the robots Figure has shipped today. You're paying for a bet that embodied AI will follow a trajectory similar to what we saw with language models, and that the company sitting in the right position when the inflection happens captures an enormous share of a market that could be measured in trillions.

The positive case rests on a few things. First, the hardware is converging. The cost of actuators, sensors, and compute has come down to the point where building a credible humanoid is no longer the bottleneck. Many teams can build the body now. What matters is the brain, and that's where the real differentiation will come from.

Second, the data flywheel. If you can get robots into factories or warehouses, even in limited roles, you start collecting real-world interaction data at scale. That data is what trains the next generation of models. The company that gets there first gets a compounding advantage that's very hard for a follower to close. That's the OpenAI playbook applied to the physical world, and investors who lived through that cycle don't want to miss it twice.

Third, the humanoid form factor itself is a strategic choice. The world is built for humans. Doors, stairs, tools, workstations. A general-purpose body that can operate in those environments without retrofitting the environment has a much larger addressable market than a specialized machine. If you believe generality wins, the humanoid is the natural endpoint.

And then there's the talent and capital argument. Figure has pulled together people from Boston Dynamics, Tesla, Google DeepMind, and they have partnerships that give them deployment channels. In a race where the winner may take most of the market, being well-funded and well-staffed early is itself part of the thesis. The valuation becomes partly self-fulfilling because it lets you attract the next round of talent and the next set of customers.

So the bull case is essentially: this is a foundation-model-style race in the physical world, the timeline is five to ten years rather than twenty, and Figure is one of a handful of companies positioned to be a winner. If you believe those three things, 30 or 40 billion is not crazy. It's an option on a very large outcome.

The honest caveat is that every one of those assumptions could be wrong on timing. Reliability in unstructured environments is still a hard problem, and the gap between a compelling demo and a robot that works ninety-nine point nine percent of the time on a factory floor is enormous. But that's what the valuation is pricing. It's not a discounted cash flow. It's a probability-weighted bet on a very large prize.

r001.rationale: The response says the addressable market could be measured in trillions and discusses factory deployment, but it does not argue that the company’s own long-term valuation could reach trillions if its robots perform production-line work.

astra-6.text:
I think the positive case starts with the idea that a humanoid robot could become a general-purpose platform for physical work. You’re not valuing it as a company that sells one machine for one narrowly defined task. You’re valuing the possibility that the same hardware, with increasingly capable intelligence, can perform many different tasks across factories, warehouses, and eventually other environments.

If that works, the addressable market is enormous. Customers would compare the robot’s cost with the value of the work it can reliably do. And if the company can earn recurring revenue from software or services, rather than just a margin on hardware, the economics could become very attractive.

The other part of the bullish case is a learning advantage: more deployed robots generate more experience, that experience improves the system, and a better system attracts more customers. If that cycle is strong, an early leader could build a durable advantage.

But those are assumptions, not conclusions. You have to believe the robots will become reliable enough, that manufacturing and servicing costs will fall, and that the company will capture a meaningful share of the value. A huge labor market doesn’t automatically translate into huge profits for a robot manufacturer.

So I would understand a thirty- or forty-billion-dollar valuation as pricing in a substantial chance of becoming a major platform for physical labor. That is the positive case. Whether it is a good investment at that price depends on how likely you think that outcome is, how long it takes, and how much additional capital is needed to get there.

r001.rationale: The response describes a large potential market and a major platform for physical labor, but it does not argue for a valuation in the trillions or specifically condition that valuation on performing production-line work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the positive case starts with a very large assumption: that a humanoid robot can become a general-purpose worker. If you believe that, you’re valuing a potential platform for physical labor, and the addressable market could be enormous.

The key is whether the economics work for the customer. How much useful work can the robot do, how reliably can it do it, and what does that cost after maintenance, supervision, and downtime? A robot doesn’t have to do everything a human can do to create value. It could start with a few repeatable tasks and expand from there.

The optimistic argument is that those deployments create a learning cycle: more robots doing real work generate more experience, which improves the system, which makes more deployments economical. If Figure can turn that into a durable advantage, investors could see a path to a very large business.

But a 30 or 40 billion dollar valuation already gives substantial credit for that future. A huge labor market alone doesn’t justify it. You also have to believe the company can deliver reliable autonomy, manufacture at scale, and retain attractive margins as competition develops. So I can understand the positive case, but understanding the opportunity and believing the price is attractive are two separate judgments.

r001.rationale: The response describes a potentially enormous market and a path to a very large business, but it does not argue for a long-term valuation in the trillions or specifically condition that valuation on robots performing production-line work.
